  2. arctan⁡\arctanarctan is the inverse of tan⁡\tantan restricted to (−π2,π2)\bigl(-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\bigr)(−2π​,2π​). State its domain and range, explain why y=±π2y=\pm\tfrac{\pi}{2}y=±2π​ are horizontal asymptotes and why arctan⁡\arctanarctan is odd, evaluate arctan⁡0\arctan 0arctan0 and arctan⁡1\arctan 1arctan1, and sketch y=arctan⁡xy=\arctan xy=arctanx.

Evaluate arcsin⁡12\arcsin\tfrac12arcsin21​, arccos⁡(−12)\arccos\bigl(-\tfrac12\bigr)arccos(−21​), arccot⁡0\operatorname{arccot}0arccot0 and arccot⁡1\operatorname{arccot}1arccot1, and give the horizontal asymptotes of y=arccot⁡xy=\operatorname{arccot}xy=arccotx.

Each inverse trigonometric function inverts one branch, and inverting swaps domain and range. Its value at a point is the one angle in that branch with the right sine, cosine, tangent or cotangent.

For arccos⁡(−12)\arccos(-\tfrac12)arccos(−21​), use cos⁡(π−θ)=−cos⁡θ\cos(\pi-\theta)=-\cos\thetacos(π−θ)=−cosθ to stay inside [0,π][0,\pi][0,π]. arccot⁡\operatorname{arccot}arccot takes its values in (0,π)(0,\pi)(0,π), so its asymptotes are the ends of that branch.

problems.html:
1. Prove that a strictly increasing function is injective.

  2. Give an injective function on [0,2][0,2][0,2] that is not monotonic.
hints: Injective means equal outputs force equal inputs. It is easier to prove the equivalent form: different inputs give different outputs.
If x1<x2x_1<x_2x1​<x2​ then strict increase gives f(x1)<f(x2)f(x_1)<f(x_2)f(x1​)<f(x2​), and in particular the two values are not equal.
For (b) you want a function that rises then falls yet never repeats a value — arrange for the two pieces to land in output sets that do not overlap.

problems.html: Prove that 3\sqrt 33​ is irrational, imitating the proof for 2\sqrt22​ in the notes. (Every integer has the form 3m3m3m, 3m+13m+13m+1 or 3m+23m+23m+2.)
hints: Set up the same contradiction as for 2\sqrt22​: suppose 3=p/q\sqrt3=p/q3​=p/q with p,qp,qp,q sharing no common factor, and square both sides.
From p2=3q2p^2=3q^2p2=3q2, p2p^2p2 is a multiple of 333. Use the hint in the question: square 3m+13m+13m+1 and 3m+23m+23m+2 and look at the remainder each leaves on division by 333.
So p=3kp=3kp=3k for some integer kkk; substitute back to get q2=3k2q^2=3k^2q2=3k2 and run the same argument on qqq. Then look at what you have shown about a common factor.

questions.stem: Which is the correct interval notation for {x∈R:x≥3}\left\{x\in\mathbb{R} : x\ge 3\right\}{x∈R:x≥3}?
options: [3,∞][3,\infty][3,∞]
(3,∞)(3,\infty)(3,∞)
(3,∞](3,\infty](3,∞]
[3,∞)[3,\infty)[3,∞)
questions.hint: Take the two ends separately, and ask of each one: is that endpoint itself a real number, and does the condition x≥3x\ge3x≥3 admit it?
questions.why: The two ends are decided by different considerations. At the left, 333 is a genuine real number and the condition x≥3x\ge 3x≥3 admits it, so that end is closed and takes a square bracket — which rules out (3,∞)(3,\infty)(3,∞). At the right, ∞\infty∞ is not a real number at all; it is shorthand for 'grows without bound', so it can never be an element of the set. A boundary at ∞\infty∞ therefore always takes a round bracket, which rules out [3,∞][3,\infty][3,∞].

questions.stem: To solve 2x+1x−3≥0\dfrac{2x+1}{x-3}\ge 0x−32x+1​≥0, a student multiplies both sides by x−3x-3x−3. What is wrong with that step?
options: An inequality may only be multiplied by a whole number.
Nothing is wrong, provided the answer is checked at the end.
The step loses the solution x=3x=3x=3.
The sign of x−3x-3x−3 is unknown, and multiplying by a negative number reverses the inequality.
questions.hint: Run the step twice — once assuming x>3x>3x>3, once assuming x<3x<3x<3 — and check whether the inequality sign survives both.
questions.why: You may add or subtract anything, and you may multiply or divide by a positive number, but multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality sign. Here x−3x-3x−3 is negative for x<3x<3x<3 and positive for x>3x>3x>3, so no single step can serve both cases, and the student's answer will be wrong on half the line. The safe route is a sign table on the intervals cut out by the zero x=−12x=-\tfrac12x=−21​ and the pole x=3x=3x=3. (Note x=3x=3x=3 is not a lost solution — it is excluded, because the expression is undefined there.)

questions.stem: As a map R→R\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}R→R, f(x)=x2f(x)=x^2f(x)=x2 is neither injective nor surjective. What happens to the same rule as a map [0,∞)→[0,∞)[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)[0,∞)→[0,∞)?
options: It becomes bijective, with inverse f−1(x)=xf^{-1}(x)=\sqrt{x}f−1(x)=x​.
It becomes surjective, but is still not injective.
Nothing changes — injectivity and surjectivity are properties of the formula alone.
It becomes injective, but is still not surjective.
questions.hint: A function is its rule together with its domain and codomain. Ask what the old objection f(−1)=f(1)f(-1)=f(1)f(−1)=f(1) is worth once −1-1−1 has left the domain.
questions.why: A function is its rule together with its domain and codomain, and changing those can change the verdict. Squaring is strictly increasing on [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞), so no two inputs share an output and it is injective — the pair f(−1)=f(1)f(-1)=f(1)f(−1)=f(1) that broke injectivity is no longer available, because −1-1−1 has left the domain. Its outputs fill [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞) exactly, which is the stated codomain, so it is also surjective. Being both, it is bijective, and the inverse is the non-negative square root.

questions.stem: With f(x)=xf(x)=\sqrt{x}f(x)=x​ and g(x)=1−x2g(x)=1-x^2g(x)=1−x2, the composite (g∘f)(x)(g\circ f)(x)(g∘f)(x) simplifies to 1−x1-x1−x. What is its domain?
options: [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞), because x\sqrt{x}x​ has to exist before ggg can act.
(0,∞)(0,\infty)(0,∞), since x=0x=0x=0 makes the square root vanish.
[−1,1][-1,1][−1,1], the domain of f∘gf\circ gf∘g.
R\mathbb{R}R, since 1−x1-x1−x is defined for every real number.
questions.hint: Read the composite in the order it acts: before ggg can do anything at all, x\sqrt{x}x​ has to exist.
questions.why: The domain of a composite is not read off the simplified formula. For g(f(x))g(f(x))g(f(x)) to mean anything, xxx must first be a legal input to fff, so x≥0x\ge 0x≥0 — and every such value is then acceptable to ggg. The cancellation that turns 1−(x)21-(\sqrt{x})^21−(x​)2 into 1−x1-x1−x hides that restriction but does not remove it. Note also that 000 is perfectly legal: 0=0\sqrt{0}=00​=0 is defined. The interval [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1] belongs to the other composite, f∘gf\circ gf∘g, which needs 1−x2≥01-x^2\ge 01−x2≥0.

questions.stem: How is the graph of y=f(x−2)y=f(x-2)y=f(x−2) related to the graph of y=f(x)y=f(x)y=f(x)?
options: Moved left by 222 — the minus sign shifts it in the negative direction.
Moved right by 222.
Squeezed towards the yyy-axis by a factor of 222.
Moved down by 222.
questions.hint: If the old graph had a feature at x=ax=ax=a, solve x−2=ax-2=ax−2=a to find where the new one has it.
questions.why: Changes inside the bracket act on the input, and therefore act backwards from how they read. To get the same output the new function needed, x−2x-2x−2 must equal the old input: if the old graph had a feature at x=ax=ax=a, the new one has it at x=a+2x=a+2x=a+2, which is to the right. Changes outside fff are the ones that behave as written — f(x)−2f(x)-2f(x)−2 really does move the graph down by 222 — and a factor inside the bracket, as in f(2x)f(2x)f(2x), is what compresses it horizontally.

questions.stem: Given arctan⁡1=π4\arctan 1=\tfrac{\pi}{4}arctan1=4π​, how many solutions does tan⁡x=1\tan x=1tanx=1 have in [0,2π)[0,2\pi)[0,2π)?
options: Two, spaced π\piπ apart.
Two, spaced 2π2\pi2π apart.
One — the inverse function returns the solution.
Infinitely many.
questions.hint: arctan⁡\arctanarctan hands back one value. Write down the period of tan⁡\tantan — it is not 2π2\pi2π — and count how many of π4+kπ\tfrac{\pi}{4}+k\pi4π​+kπ land in [0,2π)[0,2\pi)[0,2π).
questions.why: An inverse trigonometric function returns a single value, taken from the one branch on which the original function was inverted; the equation itself has as many solutions as the periodicity allows, and reading only the principal value off a calculator is the standard way to lose them. Since tan⁡\tantan has period π\piπ — not 2π2\pi2π — the second solution is π4+π=5π4\tfrac{\pi}{4}+\pi=\tfrac{5\pi}{4}4π​+π=45π​, and the next one, 9π4\tfrac{9\pi}{4}49π​, falls outside the stated range. Over all of R\mathbb{R}R there really are infinitely many, but the question fixes a window.

questions.stem: f(x)=x+4f(x)=\sqrt{x+4}f(x)=x+4​ has maximal domain [−4,∞)[-4,\infty)[−4,∞) and range [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞). Which statement about f−1f^{-1}f−1 is correct?
options: f−1(x)=x2−4f^{-1}(x)=x^{2}-4f−1(x)=x2−4 with domain [−4,∞)[-4,\infty)[−4,∞) and range [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞) — the same domain and range as fff.
f−1(x)=1x+4f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x+4}}f−1(x)=x+4​1​, since the −1-1−1 is an exponent.
f−1(x)=x2−4f^{-1}(x)=x^{2}-4f−1(x)=x2−4 with domain [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞) and range [−4,∞)[-4,\infty)[−4,∞), and its graph is the reflection of the graph of fff in the line y=xy=xy=x.
f−1(x)=x2−4f^{-1}(x)=x^{2}-4f−1(x)=x2−4 with domain [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞), and its graph is the reflection of the graph of fff in the xxx-axis.
questions.hint: Write y=x+4y=\sqrt{x+4}y=x+4​ and solve for xxx. Then ask what f−1f^{-1}f−1 is allowed to be given: its inputs are whatever fff was able to produce.
questions.why: An inverse undoes the original, so it takes fff's outputs back to fff's inputs — domain and range swap. Solving y=x+4y=\sqrt{x+4}y=x+4​ gives x=y2−4x=y^{2}-4x=y2−4, so the rule is x2−4x^{2}-4x2−4, but only on [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞): the formula x2−4x^{2}-4x2−4 by itself would accept every real number, and it is the range of fff that decides what f−1f^{-1}f−1 may be handed. The reflection is in y=xy=xy=x, because reflecting in that line is exactly what exchanges input and output; reflecting in the xxx-axis produces −f(x)-f(x)−f(x), which is a different function altogether. And f−1f^{-1}f−1 is not a reciprocal — the notation is a standing trap. Here f−1(0)=−4f^{-1}(0)=-4f−1(0)=−4, whereas 1/f(0)=121/f(0)=\tfrac121/f(0)=21​.

questions.stem: Is f(x)=x2+xf(x)=x^{2}+xf(x)=x2+x, on all of R\mathbb{R}R, even, odd, or neither?
options: Even, since x2x^{2}x2 is even and adding xxx cannot destroy the symmetry.
Neither.
Odd, since xxx is odd and x2x^{2}x2 is symmetric about the yyy-axis anyway.
Both, since it is the sum of an even function and an odd function.
questions.hint: There is only one test. Compute f(−x)f(-x)f(−x), then compare it with f(x)f(x)f(x) and with −f(x)-f(x)−f(x) — and note that failing the first comparison does not settle the second.
questions.why: Substituting gives f(−x)=x2−xf(-x)=x^{2}-xf(−x)=x2−x. That is not f(x)=x2+xf(x)=x^{2}+xf(x)=x2+x, so fff is not even; and it is not −f(x)=−x2−x-f(x)=-x^{2}-x−f(x)=−x2−x either, so fff is not odd. It is neither, which is the ordinary case — most functions have no symmetry at all, and "not even" never implies "odd". Being a sum of an even part and an odd part does not make a function both: only the zero function is both even and odd. Every function on a symmetric domain splits that way, which is a useful decomposition rather than a symmetry of the sum.

questions.stem: What is the maximal domain of f(x)=x−2x−5f(x)=\dfrac{\sqrt{x-2}}{x-5}f(x)=x−5x−2​​?
options: R∖{5}\mathbb{R}\setminus\{5\}R∖{5} — only division by zero has to be excluded.
[2,5)∪(5,∞)[2,5)\cup(5,\infty)[2,5)∪(5,∞).
[2,∞)[2,\infty)[2,∞) — the square root is the only thing that can fail.
(2,5)∪(5,∞)(2,5)\cup(5,\infty)(2,5)∪(5,∞) — the square root needs x−2>0x-2>0x−2>0.
questions.hint: Two separate things in this formula can fail. Write down the condition each one imposes, keep only the inputs meeting both, and then test the endpoint x=2x=2x=2 by substituting it.
questions.why: The maximal domain is the largest set of real inputs for which the formula makes sense, and here two conditions apply at once: the even root needs x−2≥0x-2\ge 0x−2≥0, and the denominator needs x−5≠0x-5\ne 0x−5=0. Keeping the inputs that satisfy both gives x≥2x\ge2x≥2 with x=5x=5x=5 removed, which is written [2,5)∪(5,∞)[2,5)\cup(5,\infty)[2,5)∪(5,∞). Each of the other answers drops one of the two conditions or mishandles the endpoint: x=2x=2x=2 is perfectly legal, because 0=0\sqrt{0}=00​=0 is defined and the denominator there is −3-3−3, so f(2)=0f(2)=0f(2)=0. It is only an even root of a negative number that fails, not of zero.

questions.stem: HHH is the Heaviside step: H(x)=0H(x)=0H(x)=0 for x<0x<0x<0 and H(x)=1H(x)=1H(x)=1 for x>0x>0x>0. What does H(x−1)−H(x−3)H(x-1)-H(x-3)H(x−1)−H(x−3) describe?
options: A pulse: the value 111 for 1<x<31<x<31<x<3, and 000 outside that interval.
Nothing: far to the right both steps equal 111, so the difference is 000 everywhere.
A step up at x=1x=1x=1 that never comes back down.
A pulse of height 222 on 1<x<31<x<31<x<3.
questions.hint: Take one value from each of the three regions — left of 111, between 111 and 333, right of 333 — and evaluate the two steps separately at each.
questions.why: Test the three regions. For x<1x<1x<1 neither step has switched on, and 0−0=00-0=00−0=0. For 1<x<31<x<31<x<3 the first is on and the second is not, giving 1−0=11-0=11−0=1. For x>3x>3x>3 both are on, and 1−1=01-1=01−1=0 again. So a pair of steps carves out a pulse of height 111 on 1<x<31<x<31<x<3 — the standard way to build a finite barrier or a rectangular signal, and what the potential-barrier problems on the sheet are doing. The height is 111 rather than 222 because the steps are subtracted. They do cancel far to the right, but only there.
